Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National | Opinion Ghana’s 24-Hour/New Economy: Why warehouse efficiency must drive productivity and supply chain resilience Source : Benjamin Yaw Kokroko 23 November 2026 10:23am Benjamin Yaw Kokroko ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
Ghana's 24-hour/New Economy initiative presents an opportunity to boost industrial productivity, create employment, and strengthen the country's competitiveness whether private sector or government led. However, its success will depend not only on how long businesses operate, but also on how efficiently they manage the chains of production, stock, warehousing, and distribution, which are inseparably linked.
A factory may operate around the clock, but if raw materials arrive late, stock records are inaccurate, or finished products cannot reach customers on time, additional working hours may increase operating costs without delivering proportional productivity gains.
This raises an important question: Are Ghanaian businesses operationally prepared to support a 24-hour economy?
According to Ghana's 24-Hour Economy Secretariat, 33 manufacturing companies, 268 fuel stations, and approximately 11 state enterprises had introduced multi-shift operations as of October 2026. These developments represent progress in expanding operating hours, but sustained productivity will require more than additional shifts or hours.
Warehouses and distribution centres must become central to this transformation.
Warehouses connect suppliers, manufacturers, retailers, and consumers. Their efficiency directly influences production continuity, order fulfilment, and customer satisfaction.
Yet, warehouse inefficiencies can remain hidden within daily operations. Poor inventory placement, excessive movement of warehouse personnel, inaccurate stock records, and inconsistent work procedures can increase operating costs and delay deliveries.
Consider a warehouse where frequently requested products are stored far from picking and dispatch areas. Employees may spend considerable time moving between storage locations rather than completing orders.
Introducing additional shifts without correcting these inefficiencies simply extends the same operational problems across more working hours and shifts.
For Ghanaian manufacturers, retailers, agricultural processors, and distributors, improving warehouse efficiency should therefore be a priority alongside expanding production capacity.
One practical solution is adopting data-driven warehouse management.
Rather than relying entirely on experience or assumptions, businesses can monitor operational indicators such as order lines picked per labour hour, inventory accuracy, order-processing time, and workforce utilisation levels.
These measurements help managers identify bottlenecks, evaluate employee productivity, and allocate resources more effectively.
For example, declining order-picking productivity may indicate poor product placement, equipment delays, insufficient staffing, or inefficient work assignments.
Digital tools such as warehouse management systems and Microsoft Power BI dashboards can transform operational records into useful information for decision-making.
Importantly, businesses do not necessarily need expensive technology to begin. Smaller Ghanaian enterprises can use structured inventory records, spreadsheets, barcode systems, and basic productivity reports to monitor performance.
The objective is simple: measure operational performance, identify inefficiencies, implement improvements, and evaluate results.
Warehouse layout is another critical determinant of operational efficiency.
In my published research, in the International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology (IJSRT), Warehouse Layout Design Maximization of Storage Efficiency Minimization of Travel Distances Using Simulation Models and Optimization Algorithms , I investigated how simulation and optimization techniques could improve warehouse design.
My computational experiments demonstrated potential reductions in total travel distance of up to 32%, while maintaining storage-space utilisation of up to 85% under the modelled conditions.
Although these findings do not guarantee identical results in every warehouse, they demonstrate the value of systematic layout planning.
For Ghanaian businesses, the practical implications are significant.
Frequently requested products should be positioned closer to picking and dispatch areas. Storage locations should reflect product demand and movement frequency, while aisles and material-handling pathways should support safe, efficient movement.
Such improvements can reduce unnecessary travel, improve order-processing speed, and help businesses make better use of existing warehouse infrastructure.
Warehouse productivity alone is insufficient if businesses cannot respond effectively to disruptions.
Supply chains remain vulnerable to transportation delays, supplier failures, equipment breakdowns, power interruptions, and sudden changes in demand.
These risks become particularly important when businesses operate multiple shifts and depend on continuous material availability.
In another published study in IJSRT, Risk Assessment Models Identify Potential Supply Chain Disruptions Through Scenario Analysis Monte Carlo Simulation Predictive Analytics , my co-authors and I examined how quantitative methods can support proactive supply chain risk management. The hybrid analytical approaches examined achieved predictive accuracy ranging from 76% to 86% under the study's evaluated conditions.
The central lesson is that businesses should identify operational vulnerabilities before disruptions occur.
Ghanaian companies can strengthen resilience by monitoring supplier performance, maintaining accurate inventory information, identifying critical materials, and developing alternative sourcing and distribution arrangements.
For businesses with advanced analytical capabilities, predictive models and simulation techniques can provide additional support for assessing potential disruptions.
Warehouse and distribution facilities in the United States also face challenges involving labour productivity, excessive picker travel, inventory discrepancies, fulfilment accuracy, and supply chain disruptions.
Practical solutions such as standardised operating procedures, optimised product placement, digital performance dashboards, and preventive risk management can be adapted across different warehouse environments.
However, implementation must reflect each facility's operating conditions, workforce capabilities, product characteristics, and technological resources.
The goal should not be to copy international warehouse systems without modification, but to adopt proven operational principles and measure their effectiveness locally.
To support efficient operations under the 24-hour economy, businesses should consider five practical measures:
First, establish productivity benchmarks. Measure order-processing rates, inventory accuracy, and workforce utilisation before expanding operations.
Second, optimise warehouse layouts. Position frequently requested products strategically to reduce unnecessary movement and improve material flow.
Third, adopt appropriate digital tools. Use inventory systems, barcode technologies, and performance dashboards to improve operational visibility.
Fourth, standardise warehouse procedures. Introduce clear work instructions, employee training, and structured shift handovers to ensure consistency across operating hours.
Finally, strengthen disruption preparedness. Monitor supply chain vulnerabilities and develop contingency plans to maintain operational continuity.
These improvements should be implemented progressively, with results measured against established performance indicators.
Ghana's 24-hour economy offers an opportunity to strengthen industrial development and distribution capabilities. However, longer operating hours alone cannot guarantee higher productivity.
Sustainable progress requires businesses to improve how goods are received, stored, processed, and distributed.
By investing in warehouse optimisation, operational data analytics, workforce development, and supply chain resilience, Ghanaian businesses can improve efficiency while preparing for the demands of expanded economic activity.
Ultimately, the success of a 24-hour economy should be measured not simply by how many hours businesses operate, but by how efficiently and reliably they deliver value.
Benjamin Yaw Kokroko is a warehouse operations professional and published researcher with a Master of Science in Operations and Supply Chain Analytics from Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI), USA. His research focuses on warehouse optimisation, operational data analytics, order-fulfilment efficiency, and supply chain resilience.
